vignette:
Darnell was 25, African American, and had built his life around being the one who noticed what others missed. As a journalist, he was used to moving through crowded streets, train platforms, and unfamiliar neighborhoods with a reporter’s alertness, and he had always taken pride in that ease. That changed one night after he was stopped by police on his way home from a late assignment. What began as a routine check quickly became frighteningly humiliating: a patrol car pulled in close, an officer ordered him out, and the tone shifted from clipped questions to hard suspicion. Darnell said the memory is still not organized like an ordinary recollection; it comes back with the force of being there again, more real and vivid than anything in daily life. He can still hear the footsteps coming up behind him on the pavement, the sound of boots closing the distance, and when he tries to explain the encounter he loses the thread and cannot finish, as if the scene breaks apart under his mouth. Since then, footsteps behind or nearby have become a potent jolt, and certain songs that were playing in his car earlier that evening can suddenly make his stomach drop, because they carry him back to the whole night in one instant. After those moments, he has come to scan the world as if danger is always a step away: he frequently looks behind him to check whether someone is following him, avoids unfamiliar places because he cannot assess the danger there, and finds it hard to concentrate long enough to read or draft copy without drifting back to the possibility of being cornered. He now wears concealing clothing, choosing darker, looser layers that make him feel less noticeable, and he has noticed that the more he hides, the more he convinces himself he is the kind of person who needs to hide. Darnell had also always associated journalism with curiosity and openness, but after the stop he began to tell himself that his life had been destroyed by the trauma, that he was no longer capable of doing the things that defined him, and that he used to be a happy person but now was always miserable. Those appraisals did not stay abstract; they made him pull back from the parts of life that once gave it texture. He started avoiding anything that reminded him of someone he had lost, including a close friend who had died the previous year, because grief already felt too close to the same rawness as the police encounter, and he made a point of avoiding anything that could cause negative or positive feelings alike, as though numbness were the only safe state left. Yet the more he shut down, the more convinced he became that he had already become less than himself, and that conviction deepened his misery.

The loop tightened in the weeks that followed. When he heard footsteps in the hallway outside his apartment or behind him on the sidewalk, the old scene would surge back with such vividness that he felt he had no choice but to change course, cross the street, keep his head down, or dress in a way that drew no attention. But those same protective habits kept feeding the fear. Concealing clothing made him feel hidden, yet also more on guard; avoiding unfamiliar places shrank his world and made every outing feel like a test he might fail; and cutting himself off from anything that stirred feeling left him flat and disconnected, which he then read as further proof that his life had been ruined. He noticed that once he had spent an hour checking behind him, or replaying the stop in his head, the memory became even more intrusive, almost as if the body had learned to summon it. Then the memory itself would sharpen the threat: he would hear the same footsteps in his mind, the same harsh cadence of the officers, and the remembered sounds would make the present street feel charged with danger. From there his thoughts would turn again to what the trauma meant about him—that he was not as capable as he had been, that the work that used to define him was slipping away, that he had become someone miserable and diminished—and with each return to that conclusion he became even more vigilant and more determined to avoid anything that might stir him up.

By the time he sought help, Darnell’s world had narrowed around these routines. His relationship had become strained by his withdrawal and emotional flatness, and at work he was increasingly unable to keep his attention on interviews in noisy public spaces or to move freely through the city the way his job required. What brought him in was the fear that his life was continuing to contract, that every month he was becoming more cautious, more isolated, and less like the journalist and partner he once believed himself to be. He wanted relief, but what frightened him most was the sense that one set of footsteps, one song, or one unexpected turn down an unfamiliar block could pull him straight back into that night and confirm that he was no longer the person he had been.
